newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea seen unlikely to meet '97 economic target.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea seen unlikely to meet '97 economic target.

text.p: South Korean finance minister Han Seung-soo said on Thursday the country was not expected to meet its 1997 economic targets because of an export slowdown, high costs and low efficiency.
"It will be rather difficult to attain the economic performance that we had initially forecast earlier this year," Han told members of the Seoul Foreign Correspondents' Club.
Economic growth in 1996 has been revised to around seven percent from a real 9.0 percent a year earlier.

The consumer price index grew by 4.4 percent in the first eight months of the year, close to the target of 4.5 percent for the whole year. And the current account deficit is now predicted to surpass $15 billion from an originally forecast $6.4 billion. Han said the shortfall "is not likely to improve significantly next year".
Han said cyclical problems were partly to blame. Corporate profitability has been hit hard by sharp drops in the prices of major export items.
But he said the root problem was structural.
"Our wages have been increasing at a faster rate than in competing countries, and the corporate financial burden grows larger as high interest rates continue," Han said.
Interest rates are among the highest in the world with benchmark three-year yields are now at 12.11 percent and wages growth has been in double-digits for several years.
Han added that logistical costs and land prices in South Korea were considerably higher than those in most other countries and government regulations were hobbling business.

"These structural problems have been manifest for many years, but the recent depreciation of the yen and the drop in major export prices have made them more conspicuous as major obstacles to our economy's progress," Han said.
He said the government would stress economic stability by curbing inflation and boosting corporate health.
Han said joining the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) would help accelerate Korean economic deregulation and improve economic structural problems.
Despite criticism over Korea's entry into the OECD as premature, Han said the government "stands firm in our pursuit of accession to the OECD".
